text: A hardcoded credential exists in the notebook's revision history, on anyone's screen looking at that cell, and in any copy of the code. Secret scopes exist so the value never has to appear in notebook code at all.

A Key Vault-backed scope points Databricks at a reference to the vault — its DNS name and resource ID — not a copy of any secret. Key Vault's own access policies, rotation, and audit trail govern it; Databricks is just a consumer.

A Databricks-backed scope is simplest — the value lives in Databricks-managed encrypted storage. A Key Vault-backed scope matters when a secret already has to be managed by an existing enterprise process, governed once instead of duplicated.

dbutils.secrets.get() returns the real value because the connection genuinely needs it. But Databricks automatically redacts a known secret value in notebook output, so an accidental print doesn't leak it — a safety net, not a substitute for keeping it out of the code.
Two scope types, one rule either way: the value never lives as literal text in your code. Next up: tying audit logs, lineage, and access control together into a real compliance story.
